name: Draupnir
powers: Drips eight equal rings every ninth night.
description: The gold ring of Odin, forged by Brokkr and Sindri as part of the same wager that produced Mjölnir. Every ninth night, eight rings of equal weight drip from it. When Baldr was laid on his funeral pyre, Odin laid Draupnir on the pyre, but the ring was returned from Hel by Baldr's brother Hermóðr and later burned with Baldr's wife Nanna.

name: Drómi and Leyding
powers: Failed bindings; only the silken dwarf-made fetter Gleipnir finally held Fenrir.
description: The two fetters with which the gods first tried to bind the wolf Fenrir. The first, Leyding, the wolf snapped as easily as if it were a cord. The stronger Drómi held him briefly until he braced his feet against the ground and shattered it, sending the fragments flying. Only the silken dwarf-made fetter Gleipnir was strong enough to hold him until Ragnarök.

name: Draumstafir
powers: Drawn so the sleeper receives good or revealing dreams.
description: Draumstafir, the dream stave of the Huld manuscript, a complex magical sign drawn so that the sleeper receives good or revealing dreams. It is one of the many galdrastafir recorded by 19th-century collectors of Icelandic folk magic, and the sign is still reproduced in books and tattoos, though the drawing instructions vary between grimoires.

name: Dala Horse
maker: Carvers of the Mora region, Dalarna
description: The Dala horse (Dalahäst), the carved wooden horse of Dalarna, painted in red, white, blue, and green with a floral saddle. The craft grew from toys carved during long winter evenings in the 17th century into a famous local industry around Mora, where the horses are still hand-carved and painted. The Dala horse has become the best-known symbol of Swedish craft.

name: Dejbjerg Wagon
description: The frame of a Celtic-style ceremonial wagon found in the Dejbjerg bog in West Jutland, Denmark, in 1881. Its richly ornamented bronze fittings show Mediterranean-influenced art, and it was probably the wagon of a chieftain, used in procession and then sacrificed in the bog. The wagon is exhibited in the National Museum of Denmark and is among the finest Celtic imports found in Scandinavia.

name: The Danevirke
description: A system of ramparts, walls, and moats running across the base of Jutland at Schleswig, built from the 5th century onward to guard the southern border of Denmark. It was manned and rebuilt at many points in its history and is described in the English royal chronicle of Æthelweard. The surviving stretches are a UNESCO World Heritage site, partly preserved under the modern border.

name: Wings of Daedalus
material: Feathers bound with wax and thread
powers: Carried Daedalus and Icarus off Crete; deadly when the wax melts in the sun's heat.
description: The feathered wings Daedalus built from wax and thread for himself and his son Icarus to escape the labyrinth of Crete; Icarus flew too near the sun, the wax melted, and he fell into the sea. Ovid's Metamorphoses gives the fullest telling, and the wings became the symbol of doomed invention.

name: Dyrnwyn
powers: Burst into flame when drawn by a worthy man; burned the unworthy bearer.
description: Dyrnwyn, the sword of Rhydderch Hael, one of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain. Drawn by a worthy man it burst into flame; drawn by an unworthy bearer it burned the wielder himself. A noble warrior is said to have taken it, though later tradition preserves few details of its fate.
source: Medieval Welsh list of the Thirteen Treasures of the Island of Britain

name: Durendal
powers: Indestructible blade whose pommel holds relics of Saint Peter, Saint Basil and Saint Denis.
description: Durendal, Roland's sword in the eleventh-century Chanson de Roland. Its gilded pommel holds a tooth of Saint Peter, blood of Saint Basil and hair of Saint Denis. Wounded at Roncevaux, Roland tries to break it against a rock rather than let it fall to the Saracens; the blade survives and the rock splits.

name: Cauldron of the Dagda
powers: No company ever went away from it unsatisfied.
description: Coire an Dagda, the Dagda's cauldron, one of the four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann. It is the cauldron of plenty: no company ever went away from it unsatisfied. With the spear of Lugh, the stone of Fal and the sword of Nuada it ranks among the wonder-gifts carried into Ireland by the Old Gods.
source: Lebor Gabála Érenn; four treasures of the Tuatha Dé Danann

name: The Djed Pillar
powers: Symbol of stability and of the backbone of Osiris.
description: The columnar sign shaped like a stylized tree trunk or spinal column, symbol of stability and of Osiris, whose backbone it was said to be. Set up as a temple emblem and raised by the king in the sed festival to renew his reign, it was also worn as an amulet; in the myth Isis and Nephthys restore the god beside it. Countless faience djed amulets survive from graves.

name: The Derafsh Kaviani
material: Leather apron, gold, silk, jewels (later ornament)
maker: Kaveh the blacksmith; ornamented under Faridun
powers: Royal standard of Iran, carried before the shahs as a sign of popular revolt and kingship.
description: The leather apron of the blacksmith Kaveh, raised on a spear when he led the people of Iran against the tyrant Zahhak; the new king Faridun then adorned it with gold, silk, and jewels, and it became the royal standard of the Shahs under the name Derafsh Kaviani. The banner is retold each Newroz with Kaveh as a symbol of popular revolt and rightful rule.

name: Daruma Doll
powers: Talisman of perseverance and wish fulfillment
description: A rounded paper-mache doll modeled on Bodhidharma, the first Zen patriarch, whose hollow weighted body always rocks back upright. Bought as a talisman of perseverance, its eyes are inked one at a time as a wish is granted, and the year's dolls are burned in temple ceremonies that close out the warding of ill fortune.

name: Dreamcatcher
material: Wooden hoop with woven netting and feathers
era: Ojibwe tradition; widely copied since the 20th century
powers: Catches bad dreams in its web and lets good ones through.
description: A small hoop of willow bound with a spider-web net, hung over a cradle to catch bad dreams while good ones slip through the center hole, in Ojibwe tradition. The web form is tied to stories of the spider grandmother, and early Anishinaabe accounts record the charm for infants. Since the 1960s it has become a commercialized pan-Indian symbol, one scholars caution has drifted from its original use.
source: Ojibwe oral tradition and early ethnographic accounts

name: Duho
powers: Raises the cacique above the ground and close to the spirits.
description: The duho is the carved wooden seat of the Taíno, a ceremonial stool of guaiacum or mahogany on which caciques sat in ritual, often carved as a creature or reclining zemi figure. Spanish chroniclers recorded chiefs receiving Columbus seated on duhos; museum-dated examples from about AD 600 span the islands from Cuba to the Bahamas. It raised its user toward the spirits in cohoba ceremonies.
source: Archaeological duhos in museum collections and early colonial accounts

name: Dahomey Applique Cloth
description: Dahomey (Fon) applique cloths are rectangular textiles on which cut-out cloth figures are sewn to tell royal history and proverbs. Commissioned for the Fon court, they depict kings, warriors, and the kingdom's celebrated women soldiers, and were also carried as banners and umbrella covers in royal processions.
source: Fon court tradition; museum collections (Musée du quai Branly)

name: Dogon Kanaga Mask
description: The kanaga is a wooden headdress of the Dogon of Mali with a vertical crest and crossed bars, danced by masked societies at dama funerals and the great Sigi ceremonies. The crossed arms echo Amma's creation and the structure of the world, while the mask mediates between the living and the spirits of the dead.
source: Dogon masked society tradition; ethnographic studies (Griaule school)

name: Dan Mask
description: Dan masks of the Ivory Coast are carved wooden face masks with narrow eye slits and a smooth, reflective surface, worn at entertainment, justice, and initiation. A mask's power lies in the spirit (gle) it embodies; each is owned by a community or family and handled with ritual care, oiled and fed to keep its force alive.
